The ARC pilot plant is designed to produce 525 MW of fusion power in a compact tokamak with major radius of 3.3 m and magnetic field of 9.2 T.

Recent modeling indicates that the X-point target (XPT) divertor configuration can attain a stable, fully detached divertor state, handling upstream power densities about 10 times higher than standard vertical target divertors.
The superconducting poloidal field coils in ARC are placed inside the toroidal field magnet envelope, taking advantage of the demountable TF coil design.
Advanced neutron transport calculations show a tritium breeding ratio of ~1.08 and a 3-30 times lower neutron damage rate at the remote divertor targets compared to the first wall.
A tungsten swirl tube FLiBe coolant channel design is considered for the divertor, capable of exhausting heat fluxes up to 12 MW/m2.
The long-leg divertor geometry enables feedback control of the detachment front location using microwave interferometry.
The optical transparency of the FLiBe blanket allows diagnostics like thermal imaging of the vacuum vessel exterior and monitoring of Cherenkov radiation to infer the fusion reaction rate.
